pairs.rationale: The earlier scene describes both baptizing ministries and John's followers reporting that everyone is coming to Jesus. John4:1 continues that growing-ministry setting with the Pharisees' hearing. The target does not itself narrate the Pharisees hearing or establish the numerical comparison as an independent census.

John3:22 attributes baptizing to Jesus while mentioning His disciples;4:2 expressly clarifies that the disciples, rather than Jesus personally, performed it. This is an internal agency clarification of the earlier narrative, not a second independent witness.

Both narrate Jesus withdrawing to Galilee. Matthew gives hearing of John's handover as the occasion; John places the departure after news of Jesus' baptizing ministry reaching the Pharisees. The different triggers and chronology are not merged into one asserted journey.

Both connect a field near Shechem/Sychar with Jacob's gift to Joseph. The actual Joshua unit says Jacob acquired the Shechem field and gave it to Joseph as a portion. John locates Sychar near the plot; the link does not equate the two city names or add identification of the well itself.

Both scenes have a request for drinking water addressed to a woman at a spring. Genesis' servant asks from Rebekah's jar; John has Jesus address the Samaritan woman. The concrete encounter pattern is compared without identifying the people or making the Samaritan encounter a marriage arrangement.

Both depict a barrier between Jesus' Jewish/Jerusalem association and Samaritans. John records the woman's surprise at a Jew requesting her drink; Luke narrates another village refusing reception because of His Jerusalem destination. These are different communities and journeys; Luke does not prove a universal response by every Samaritan.

Both place the offer of living water in Jesus' speech. John7 additionally connects its water saying with the Spirit and Jesus' glorification;4:10 speaks of God's gift and knowing the speaker. The later explanation is a related Gospel passage, without inserting its whole formulation into this unit.

The woman asks how Jesus can provide the promised water without a drawing vessel; Nicodemus asks how an old person can enter a womb and be born. Both dialogues place a tangible-mechanism question beside Jesus' life-giving imagery. The water and birth images and their questioners remain different.

Both interlocutors ask whether Jesus is greater than a named father: Jacob here and Abraham in8:53. John4 invokes the ancestral well, whereas John8 invokes death and Jesus' word. This is a repeated rhetorical challenge to Jesus' significance, not an identification of the patriarchs or settings.

John4 contrasts repeatedly needed well water with Jesus' enduring gift in the following verse. John6:49–50 contrasts manna eaten by ancestors who died with heaven's bread and life. The shared temporary/enduring provision contrast is retained; food, death, water and renewed thirst are not treated as identical assertions.

Both promises explicitly say that the one receiving from Jesus will not thirst. John4 describes His water becoming a spring unto eternal life; John6 calls Him the bread of life and joins coming/believing with hunger/thirst. The different images remain visible.

The woman asks for the water Jesus has offered, just as John6's hearers ask Him always to give the offered bread. The water request adds avoiding thirst and the drawing trip; the bread request does not. This compares the dialogue responses, not identical physical provisions.

Both recipients of Jesus' disclosure or healing call Him a prophet. The Samaritan woman responds after His knowledge of her marital history; John9's healed man responds about the opening of his eyes. The two recognitions have different persons and evidential settings.

The Greek-numbered Psalm121 explicitly describes going to the Lord's house in Jerusalem and the tribes going up to give thanks. It supplies a concrete Jerusalem-worship counterpart to the woman's stated contrast. It neither names her mountain nor settles her dispute by identifying its site.

Both passages challenge confinement of divine worship or dwelling to a constructed earthly site. Jesus forecasts worship of the Father beyond the two disputed locations; Stephen says the Most High does not dwell in handmade things and quotes heaven/earth imagery. Stephen does not reproduce Jesus' hour or name the Samaritan mountain.

Romans locates covenant privileges, worship, promises and Christ's fleshly descent among Israelites. This supports comparison with the specific claim that salvation is from the Jews. It does not independently repeat Jesus' judgment about what the Samaritan hearers know.

Both describe worship associated with God's Spirit. John adds the Father seeking true worshipers in spirit and truth; Philippians joins worship by the Spirit with boasting in Christ and rejecting confidence in flesh. The formulations are related without making all their qualifications identical.

The requirement for worship in spirit has a counterpart in Philippians' worship by the Spirit of God. John additionally says God is spirit and requires truth; the target does not repeat those whole claims. This is a bounded worship comparison, not a new definition of the relationship between divine and human spirit.

Both passages explicitly identify Messiah with the title Christ. The woman anticipates His coming and instruction, whereas Andrew announces that they have found Him. The target does not repeat the woman's prediction of announcing all things.

In both settings Jesus answers an explicitly messianic context with personal affirmation. John has the woman's Messiah expectation followed by His I-am-He reply; Mark has the high priest's Christ question and Jesus' I-am answer. The private conversation and trial, and Mark's added Son-of-Man saying, remain distinct.

Both invitations ask someone to come and encounter Jesus in a messianic context. Philip says come and see after identifying the One of whom Moses and the prophets wrote; the woman says come, see a man and asks whether He is Christ. Her knowledge-of-deeds testimony is not attributed to Philip.

Jesus' unfamiliar food, explained as doing the Sender's will in4:34, is compared with His refusal to make bread alone the measure of life in Matthew's temptation scene. Matthew quotes life by God's word; it does not narrate the disciples' meal conversation or say Jesus never ate physical food.

Both identify doing the will of the One who sent Jesus as His mission. John4 calls that obedience His food and adds completing the work; John6 contrasts the Sender's will with His own and mentions descent from heaven. The shared obedience claim does not erase the different images.

Both address disciples with a harvest image for their mission. John speaks of fields ready for harvest in contrast to a four-month saying; Matthew calls the harvest plentiful and asks for workers. Matthew does not establish John's four-month detail or a literal agricultural timetable.

Both spiritual-labor passages speak of workers and wages using cultivation imagery. John describes reaping, eternal-life fruit and shared joy; Paul distinguishes planting/watering, God's growth and wages according to labor. The roles and reward descriptions are compared without assigning Paul or Apollos to John's unnamed workers.

John distinguishes sower from reaper; Paul distinguishes his planting from Apollos' watering while crediting God with growth. Both recognize distinct contributions to one cultivation work. Watering is not silently changed into reaping, and the participants are not identified across the passages.

Jesus describes entering work others have labored at; Paul describes laying a foundation on which another builds. The common feature is succeeding to another's prior ministry labor. The construction and harvest images differ, and Paul is not identified as one of the earlier workers in Jesus' saying.

The narrator repeats the woman's everything-I-did testimony already voiced in4:29 and now reports its effect on Samaritan belief. The earlier verse is invitation and question, the later verse a reception notice. This is an explicit internal return to her words, not independent corroboration of the encounter.

The Samaritan hosts ask Jesus to remain; Luke's different Samaritan village refuses Him because of His Jerusalem destination. The opposite receptions form a concrete narrative contrast involving Jesus and Samaritan communities. The two-day stay belongs only to John and no universal Samaritan attitude is inferred.

The Samaritans' further belief because of Jesus' word illustrates the word/hearing/faith connection stated in Romans. Romans supplies a general account of hearing through Christ's word, not an independent account of this city or a count of its converts.

Both expressly call Jesus/the Son Savior of the world. John4 presents the Samaritans' firsthand-hearing confession;1John presents testimony that the Father sent the Son. Their witnesses and formulations differ without narrowing the shared world-wide title to one local community.

The departure after two days closes the two-day stay explicitly reported in4:40. This internal chronological return links the end of the visit to its earlier duration statement;4:40 does not independently narrate the later departure into Galilee.

Both report Jesus' proverb about a prophet lacking honor at home. Mark adds relatives and household in a setting of offense; John places the testimony beside the Galilean welcome notice. Those contexts remain visible without forcing an identification of occasions or explaining away their differing reception.

John2 records people in Jerusalem at Passover believing after seeing signs;4:45 recalls Galileans seeing Jesus' deeds in Jerusalem at the feast before welcoming Him. This links the narrative's feast-and-seen-deeds notices. It does not identify every member of the two groups or equate welcome with the full belief claim.

John4 expressly recalls Cana's water becoming wine. John2:9–11 narrates the water-wine discovery and locates the beginning of signs in Cana. That earlier sign is the clear internal counterpart; the royal official and ill son enter the later account rather than the wedding episode.

Both fathers seek Jesus' coming because a child is near death. John's man is a royal official with a son; Mark's named synagogue ruler Jairus has a daughter and asks for laying on hands. The common urgent plea is retained without merging the families or healing journeys.

John6's hearers explicitly ask for a sign so that they may see and believe, matching the condition criticized by Jesus' plural you-all in4:48. One is a rebuke and the other a demand; the groups and occasions are not equated.

Both pleas ask Jesus to come while a little child is dying or before death. The royal official's son and Jairus' daughter remain different children, and Mark additionally asks for hands to be laid on her. Neither account is used to identify the other parent.

Both join Jesus' go command, belief and a dependent's restoration without narrating Jesus arriving at the patient. John has an official's son and a word that he lives; Matthew has a centurion's servant healed at that hour. The officials, dependents and wording are kept distinct.

Both report confirmation of a dependent's health through servants or messengers. John's slaves meet the returning father; Luke's sent people return to a house and find the slave well. The movement, patient and household relationships are different, not one harmonized scene.

Both healing accounts explicitly notice the hour of restoration. John gives the servants' yesterday/seventh-hour fever report; Matthew says the centurion's servant was healed at that hour. Matthew does not independently establish John's clock time or child, and John's next verse separately relates the hour to Jesus' word.

Both narratives join a man's belief with his whole household. John ties the father's recognition to his son's recovery at Jesus' word; Acts describes the jailer's household rejoicing after belief and baptism. The target supports the household-faith motif, not the timing or identity of John's healing.

Both sign narratives contain an ordinal notice connected with Cana/Galilee: John2 names the beginning of signs, and4:54 calls this again the second sign on the return from Judea. This marks the Gospel's narrative sign notices, not an exhaustive assertion that Jesus had performed only two signs anywhere;2:23 already mentions Jerusalem signs.

Both narrate Jesus going up to Jerusalem in connection with a Jewish feast. John2 explicitly names Passover;5:1 does not name this feast. The recurring itinerary is compared without supplying a feast identity or treating the two visits as one.

Both name a Sheep Gate in the Jerusalem setting. Nehemiah records priests building and consecrating it; John locates the Bethzatha pool near it. The shared toponym does not prove unchanged masonry or supply John's pool name, five porticoes or precise archaeological identification.

Both describe groups including blind and lame people in a healing context. Matthew's crowd brings sufferers to Jesus on the Galilean mountain; John's sufferers lie at a Jerusalem pool and the ensuing account concerns one man. Other conditions and the scope of healings are not made identical.

Both stories specify a multi-year condition before Jesus' restoration in a Sabbath setting. John's man has been ill thirty-eight years; Luke's bent woman has eighteen years of a spirit of weakness. The persons, durations, descriptions and causes remain different; no diagnosis is added to John's unit.

Both have Jesus address prospective recipients with a question about the help desired. John asks one long-ill man whether he wants to become well; Matthew asks two blind men what they wish Him to do. The wording, number and initiative differ without identifying the encounters.

John's man lacks a helper to reach the pool; Mark's paralyzed man has four bearers who overcome a crowd and roof barrier. The concrete contrast concerns human assistance in access to healing. Mark supplies no pool mechanism, and the absent John5:4 angel account is not restored to explain the stirred water.
Both commands tell a man to rise and take his mat. John adds walking; Mark tells the paralyzed man to go home. The Jerusalem-pool and Capernaum-house settings and patients remain different.

Both narrate immediate restoration followed by taking up the mat and moving. John explicitly dates the event to Sabbath; Mark's present passage does not. The parallel response does not identify the men or import John's date into Mark.

Jeremiah explicitly forbids lifting or carrying burdens on Sabbath in the Jerusalem setting. It is a concrete legal-text background to the objection to carrying the mat. The target does not itself judge Jesus' healing or establish that His opponents' application to this case was correct.

The healed man reports the take-up-and-walk command actually spoken in5:8. This is an explicit internal quotation used in his response to the objection. It does not create a second independent witness or add a moral motive for his reply.

Both healing investigations pursue how restoration happened and who was responsible. John5's question asks who gave the walking command; John9's parents answer questions about their son and say they do not know who opened his eyes. Questioners, witnesses, conditions and the stated questions differ.

Both healed men cannot provide requested information about an absent healer. John5's man does not know who He is; John9's man, who has already named Jesus, does not know where He is. The contrast preserves the different kinds of ignorance and does not claim the men had the same knowledge.

Both encounters include Jesus' instruction to sin no more. John5 addresses a restored man and adds a warning about something worse; the bracket-marked John8 passage concerns a woman accused of adultery and a non-condemnation reply. The link does not establish a cause for the man's original illness or a new critical-text verdict.

Both healed men identify Jesus as responsible for their restoration when reporting to other people. John5 follows Jesus finding the man again; John9 recounts mud, washing and restored sight. The methods and patients differ, and no betrayal motive is assigned to John5's report.

Both accounts narrate opposition to Jesus because He healed on Sabbath. John records persecution by the Jews in this scene; Luke records the synagogue ruler's indignation and crowd instruction. These are particular narrative participants and different healings, not a claim about every Jewish person.

Both relate Jesus' work to the divine Sender. John5 speaks of the Father working even now and Jesus working; John9 says we must work the Sender's works while it is day. The plural workers and day/night image in John9 are not made identical to John5's Sabbath defense.

Both connect lethal hostility with Jesus' relation to God. John5:18 gives the narrator's explanation involving Sabbath breaking and calling God His own Father, making Himself equal to God; John10:33 quotes opponents accusing Him of blasphemy and making Himself God. The different formulations and narrative attribution remain distinct, without adding a separate doctrinal ruling.

Both sayings deny autonomous action or speech from Jesus Himself and refer it to the Father. John5 concerns the Son doing what He sees the Father do; John12 concerns speaking what the sending Father commanded. Doing and speaking are related but not interchangeable formulations.

Both explicitly state that the Father loves the Son. John5 describes showing works and future greater works; John3 describes giving all things into His hand. The common love statement is direct, while the different descriptions of showing and entrusting remain intact.

Both attribute life-giving power to Jesus/the Son. John5 compares the Son's giving life with the Father raising the dead; John11 names Jesus resurrection and life and promises life to the believer despite death. Their qualifications are retained rather than replaced by a universal timetable.

John says the Father has given all judgment to the Son;2Timothy names Christ Jesus as the coming judge of living and dead. The latter gives a direct counterpart for Christ's judging role but does not restate the entire Father-to-Son grant.

Both intertwine honor directed to Jesus with God the Father. John requires honoring the Son as the Father; Philippians describes God's exaltation, knees bending and tongues confessing Jesus as Lord to the Father's glory. The particular just-as requirement and the exaltation narrative are not collapsed into one wording.

Both expressly describe passing from death into life. John5 associates this with hearing Jesus and believing His Sender;1John gives love of the brothers as the sign by which we know the transition. The passages' different conditions or evidential emphasis remain visible.

John11 narrates Jesus' loud command followed by the dead Lazarus coming out, a concrete voice-and-life counterpart. John5 speaks more broadly of the dead hearing the Son and living. One bodily restoration does not by itself settle the full meaning, scope or coming/now-is timing of that saying.

The prologue locates life in the Word, while John5 speaks of Father and Son having life in themselves and the Father giving this to the Son. The shared life-in-the-divine-person theme is compared without silently adding John5's gave formulation to the prologue.

Both associate the Son of Man with judgment. John states the granting of authority; Matthew portrays the Son of Man enthroned and separating the gathered nations. The enacted judgment scene is a counterpart for the role, not a repetition of the grant's wording.

The command at Lazarus' tomb and the dead man's emergence provide a concrete comparison for voice reaching those in tombs. John5 predicts all in the tombs hearing His voice; John11 narrates one man, not completion of the universal future event.

Both passages distinguish outcomes among those arising from death. John names resurrection of life and judgment by good/base deeds; the supplied Greek-based Daniel names everlasting life, reproach, dispersion and everlasting shame among those arising. Daniel's actual wording and many are retained rather than replaced with another edition's two-part formula.

Both deny pursuing Jesus' own will in favor of the will of the One who sent Him. John5 applies this to hearing and righteous judgment; John6 frames His heavenly descent and mission. The shared will statement does not make their full subjects identical.

Both passages explicitly discuss Jesus bearing witness concerning Himself. John5's conditional says His testimony is not true; John8 affirms its truth and adds the Father and the two-person testimony rule. The differing formulations are left visible rather than silently changing true into another term or forcing a complete harmonization.

Both introduce witness beyond Jesus' own testimony. John8 explicitly names the sending Father; the present John5 unit says Another without naming Him. The comparison marks the additional-witness pattern without establishing that identity from this isolated word alone;5:33 and5:37 supply further context.

John1 explicitly narrates people sent to John and his testimony in response. John5 recalls sending to John and his truthful testimony. This is a concrete earlier Gospel scene to compare, without assuming every individual listener in the later controversy was one of the earlier delegates.

Both explain communication as directed toward the hearers'/readers' salvation or life. Jesus says these things so they may be saved; the Gospel's ending says the written signs aim at belief and life in His name. The latter does not repeat the disclaimer about receiving human testimony.

Both use light imagery for John's witness role. John5 calls him a burning, shining lamp; the prologue expressly says he was not the Light but witnessed to it. Lamp and the true Light are not made identical, nor is John identified as Jesus.

Both expressly say Jesus' works bear witness concerning Him in relation to the Father. John5 compares that testimony with John's and speaks of completing given works; John10 says the works done in His Father's name testify. The additional qualifications remain distinct.

Both expressly attribute testimony concerning Jesus to the Father who sent Him. John5 additionally says the hearers have not heard His voice or seen His form; John8 does not repeat that accusation. No particular heavenly-voice event is supplied as an unmentioned identity for the testimony.

Both describe a divine/Jesus word failing to remain or find room in hostile hearers. John5 connects this with not believing the sent One; John8 connects it with seeking to kill Jesus. The different word formulations and responses are not erased.

Both explicitly present the Scriptures as concerning Jesus. John speaks of searching them and their witness; Luke narrates Jesus explaining Moses and the prophets concerning Himself. Luke's different audience and resurrection setting do not reproduce the accusation against John's hearers.

Both connect coming to Jesus with the life He provides. John5 rebukes unwillingness to come for life; John6 calls Him the bread of life and promises lasting provision to the one who comes/believes. Rejection and invitation remain different rhetorical functions.

Both distinguish Jesus' mission from self-directed glory seeking. John5 denies receiving glory from people; John7 contrasts a self-speaker's own glory with seeking the Sender's glory. The link does not turn these sayings into a denial that Jesus may rightly be honored.

Both portray Jesus as knowing people's inner state. John5 specifies their lack of God's love; John2 says He knew what was within a person and did not entrust Himself to the sign-believing group. The target does not independently name or diagnose every John5 listener.

Both describe Jesus' coming and failure to receive Him. John1 contrasts His own not receiving with others receiving and becoming God's children; John5 contrasts His Father's-name coming with hypothetical reception of someone in his own name. The hypothetical other is not assigned an unverified personal identity.

Both connect preference for human glory over God's glory with impaired reception of Jesus. John5 asks how such hearers can believe; John12 explicitly says some rulers believed but withheld confession because of that preference and fear. The difference between the question and the narrated hidden belief is preserved.

Deuteronomy places Moses' law book as a witness against the people and recalls their rebellion. This is concrete Mosaic accusation background for John's naming Moses as accuser. It does not narrate Moses speaking before the Father or turn the two scenes into one event.

Acts explicitly places Jesus the appointed Christ beside Moses' promised prophet and the command to hear him. It provides a specific Mosaic-prophecy comparison for Jesus' saying that Moses wrote concerning Him. John5 does not name this as the only Mosaic text intended.

Both sayings connect refusal of Moses' witness with failure to receive a further disclosure. John5 contrasts Moses' writings and Jesus' words; Luke's Abraham contrasts hearing Moses/Prophets with persuasion by someone risen. The parable's speaker and resurrection scenario remain distinct.

deferred.reason: The particular required route through Samaria has no retained precise counterpart; other Samaria journeys have different directions and circumstances.
Jacob's spring, travel weariness and the sixth-hour seating notice remain particular; no unverified well identity or generic fatigue link is credited.
This disciples' food-buying errand is a particular transition; other buying discussions do not establish the errand.
The command to call this woman's husband is a particular exchange, not reproduced by generic marriage passages.
The woman's no-husband reply and Jesus' approval remain specific to her circumstances; they are not equated with another woman's story.
The five past husbands and present non-husband are not independently identified; no allegorical identities or biography is manufactured.
The disciples' wonder and two unspoken questions remain particular; unrelated surprise at Jesus' conversation is not credited.
Leaving this water jar and going to the city remains a particular action; no symbolism for the jar or equivalent abandoned-possession claim is supplied.
The city residents' movement toward Jesus is a brief transition without a retained precise counterpart.
The disciples' request that Rabbi eat remains a particular meal-conversation prompt; unrelated eating scenes are not treated as the same action.
The question about someone bringing food remains this dialogue's specific misunderstanding; a generic food request does not reproduce it.

review_notes: Read all100 original source units in John4–5 after the recorded completion of all1149 Luke source units. Read every retained actual target passage with surrounding context; reused targets were not credited as new source reviews.

John5:4 is absent in the original and remains absent. The stirred-water statement in5:7 is not supplemented by an angel account. John8:11 retains its actual closing bracket as target evidence; no new critical-text judgment is claimed.

Psalm121 and Nehemiah and all other source divisions follow the Saints Greek-based inventory. Narrative comparisons retain the distinct royal official/son, centurion/slave, Jairus/daughter and separate Sabbath patients.
Internal references and contrasts are labeled as such, not offered as independent testimony. Named sites and unnamed witnesses are not assigned unsupported identities.
This is supplied-English passage comparison, without new Greek/Hebrew apparatus verification, exhaustive concordance or independent human specialist approval.
